title: Here’s what history class didn’t teach you about Taft
text:
Here’s what history class didn’t teach you about Taft
In the annals of the American presidency, Republican William Howard Taft is seldom celebrated or deemed a superstar. He served one term between 1909 and 1913, his reelection bid hampered by a challenge from his predecessor and former friend, Theodore Roosevelt. Taft’s sedate sensibility invited unflattering comparisons with the kinetic Roosevelt and, in the campaign of 1912, both men lost to Democrat Woodrow Wilson. Though Taft would go on to become chief justice of the United States in 1921, his legacy languishes almost like a footnote.
But in “William Howard Taft,” author Walter Stahr argues that the nation’s 27th president deserves a second look. This is the first full biography of Taft since Henry Pringle’s two-volume work in 1939. Stahr’s thoroughly researched book clocks in at nearly 700 pages. Will readers want such a deep dive into the life of a leader long considered an afterthought? It’s an audacious prospect, but as Stahr frequently suggests, Taft could be audacious, too.
That’s not the popular reputation of a man long known as the calm junior partner of the volatile Roosevelt. As Roosevelt’s secretary of war, Taft worked far beyond his portfolio, serving essentially as the president’s deputy. He’d already earned a reputation for diligence and diplomatic skill as the first American civilian governor of the Philippines. When Roosevelt opted not to run for reelection in 1908, Taft was his anointed successor. But Roosevelt grew restless out of office and mounted a bid for a comeback. His opposition to Taft in 1912 created a cataclysmic feud.
A new biography of the 27th U.S. president, who later became chief justice of the United States, argues that his best qualities have been overlooked.
Doris Kearns Goodwin explored that seismic rift in “The Bully Pulpit: Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, and the Golden Age of Journalism,” her 2013 bestseller that drew a sharp contrast between Roosevelt’s rhetorical ebullience and Taft’s tamer style. Stahr praises “The Bully Pulpit” but points out that it didn’t aspire to be a complete account of Taft’s life.
Born in Ohio to a prominent family that included a father who had served in the cabinet of Ulysses S. Grant, Taft seemed on track for a national stage. He studied law, then quickly rose to prominence in a series of public roles. Assessing his own success, Taft playfully commented that, “like every well-trained Ohio man I always had my plate the right side up when offices were falling.”
While Taft credited his ascendance to good fortune, he was also ambitious, which is one of the defining themes in Stahr’s book. He disputes the widespread observation that Taft never really wanted to be president. While Taft’s lawyerly mind made him better suited to jurisprudence, his “relentless presidential campaign in 1907 and 1908, however, shows that he was a far from reluctant candidate,” Stahr writes. To advance his candidacy, Taft crisscrossed the country by train, often sleeping upright with other passengers.
Among the skeptics about Taft’s White House accomplishments was Taft himself, who called his presidency “humdrum.”
Even so, “William Howard Taft” details a few wins within the Taft administration that have particular currency given the ongoing national conversation about trade policy and immigration. Taft worked to lower tariffs, including those imposed on Canada, and he vetoed legislation “to exclude ‘undesirable immigrants,’” Stahr notes.
“William Howard Taft” is a long book, but its size reflects a man who led two lives on the public stage. Taft remains the only person to serve as both president and chief justice, and while Stahr is measured in his view of Taft’s presidency, he gives him better marks for his work on America’s highest bench. He credits Taft with championing changes that made the Supreme Court more efficient and responsive in hearing major cases, reforms that continue to shape its work. Shortly before his death in 1930, Taft also secured support for the construction of the court’s first permanent home, the majestic building it now occupies. Stahr concludes that “no chief justice has changed the Supreme Court as much as Taft.”
In Stahr’s previous books on John Jay, William Henry Seward, Edwin Stanton, and Salmon P. Chase, he displayed a gift for bringing often overlooked historical characters into the foreground. The Taft he summons to life in these pages – amiable, self-effacing, but quietly competent – seems ripe for a reassessment. “In the end, then,” Stahr writes, “perhaps the lesson of Taft’s life for our own times may be that we need to cultivate the modest personal virtues that enabled Taft to accomplish so much for the American people.”
